entry.evidence: Our goal is to determine the age of the ice, understand its overall geologic history, and evaluate its potential use as a paleoclimate archive.

steps.action: The authors pose the question of the age and geologic history of the buried Middle ice in Ong Valley, framed by the lack of ice archives older than about 0.8-1 Ma.
steps.quote: Our goal is to determine the age of the ice, understand its overall geologic history, and evaluate its potential use as a paleoclimate archive.

steps.action: The authors take over their group's earlier surface-debris exposure ages (>1.1 Ma, likely >1.8 Ma) and the sublimation and erosion rates as the starting estimate and as initial guesses for the fit.
steps.quote: Cosmogenic nuclide measurements from the supraglacial debris suggest an age of > 1.1 Ma but most likely > 1.8 Ma (Bibby et al., 2016)

steps.action: The authors adopt the simplest working hypothesis: the Middle ice was emplaced in a single glacial advance with well-mixed englacial debris of uniform inheritance.
steps.quote: we start with the simplest assumption that the deposit of the Middle ice is from a single glacial advance

steps.action: The authors design a depth-profile sampling (pit, ice core, erratic boulders) at a central high point of the Middle drift chosen to minimize ice deformation and rockfall input.
steps.quote: We chose this site because any deformation of the buried ice should be minimized at this location

steps.action: The authors dig a 62 cm pit, drill a 944 cm debris-rich ice core with a Winkie drill, sample boulders, and describe the core visually as banded basal ice of an Argosy Glacier advance.
steps.quote: We collected a 944 cm long and 7 cm diameter vertical ice core directly below the deepest supraglacial debris sample.

steps.action: The authors build a numerical forward model (shielding mass, depth through time, spallation and muon production, decay, inheritance) that predicts nuclide concentrations with depth under the single-exposure scenario.
steps.quote: The model then predicts nuclide concentrations in supraglacial and englacial debris.

steps.action: The authors measure 10Be, 21Ne and 26Al in 6 pit samples, 12 core samples and the surface sample, and find large downcore variations including anomalously high concentrations at depth.
steps.quote: cosmogenic nuclide concentrations in the englacial debris show large downcore variations

steps.action: In the Methods, the authors check the 21Ne measurements against the CRONUS-A intercomparison standard and correct 10Be and 26Al for procedural blanks run with each batch.
steps.quote: indistinguishable from the accepted value of 320 × 10 6 atoms g - 1

steps.action: The authors measure 10Be and 21Ne in Middle drift and lateral moraine boulders and note discordant apparent ages (10Be younger than 21Ne).
steps.quote: the apparent 10 Be exposure ages reported for all boulder samples appear younger than of those from 21 Ne

steps.action: The authors compare the single-exposure prediction (monotonic decrease with depth) with the measured profile and find that sections with downcore increases are incompatible with it.
steps.quote: are therefore not compatible with a single exposure history described above

steps.action: The authors keep the forward model but revise the uniform-inheritance auxiliary: they split the samples into englacial units (S1, E1, E2) fitted by the model and recycled paleo-surface units (S2-S4) used as a burial constraint.
steps.quote: Based on the above observations we can only explain a subset of the data with the forward model.

steps.action: The authors fit the forward model to S1, E1 and E2 with fmincon and a burial constraint from S2-S4, and run a 10 000-iteration Monte Carlo to estimate emplacement age, sublimation rate, erosion rate and inheritance.
steps.quote: provide an ice emplacement age of 2.95 + 0.18 / - 0.22 Ma for the Middle ice

steps.action: The authors compare the best-fit predictions with the englacial units in depth and paired-nuclide space and separate them from the paleo-surface samples.
steps.quote: it is therefore evident that these units can be explained with the exposure model

steps.action: The authors compute an absolute minimum emplacement age under minimal assumptions (inheritance set to the minimum measured concentrations, zero erosion).
steps.quote: We find the absolute minimum exposure age of the Middle ice to be 1.331 + 0.020 / - 0.024 Ma

steps.action: The authors subtract the modelled post-depositional inventory from the paleo-surface samples and compute apparent burial ages for S2, S3 and S4 from three nuclide pairs.
steps.quote: The paleo-surface S3 and S4 indicate longer periods of burial

steps.action: The authors compare the fitted sublimation rate with earlier cosmogenic estimates in Ong Valley and elsewhere in the Transantarctic Mountains.
steps.quote: These rates broadly agree with a sublimation rate of 22.86 m Myr - 1 as reported here in Ong Valley.

steps.action: The authors reject the much higher sublimation rates from water-vapour diffusion models because the implied 300-1500 m of surface lowering conflicts with moraine elevations.
steps.quote: are inconsistent with glacial moraine elevations and field observations in Ong Valley

steps.action: The authors compare the fitted erosion rate and debris concentration with published Antarctic regolith erosion rates and Beacon Valley debris concentrations.
steps.quote: an erosion rate of 0.206 m Myr - 1 as reported here for the supraglacial debris is in agreement

steps.action: The authors vary sublimation rate, erosion rate and age to test whether the systematic misfit of the near-surface pit samples can be removed, and find that it cannot.
steps.quote: neither of these scenarios will result in a better fit for the near-surface pit samples

steps.action: The authors refine the account of the supraglacial debris by proposing partial vertical mixing driven by polygon activity, which explains the misfit and the low paired-nuclide ratios.
steps.quote: partial vertical mixing of the supraglacial debris may have occurred

steps.action: The authors solve the boulder 10Be/21Ne pairs for exposure age and steady erosion by Monte Carlo and check the result against the modelled ice age.
steps.quote: therefore agree with our modeled age of 2.96 Ma for the Middle drift ice

steps.action: The authors compare the S2 minimum burial age with the Middle ice age and interpret S2 as surface debris overridden and mixed in during the ~3 Ma advance.
steps.quote: the minimum burial age of 3.21 ± 0.20 Ma for S2 agrees with the age of the Middle ice

steps.action: To explain the older, non-uniform burial ages of S3 and S4, the authors propose an older ice mass, with two rivals left open: older ice stratigraphically under the Middle ice, or older ice entrained into it.
steps.quote: the Middle ice advanced over an already existing ice-cored drift unit

steps.action: The authors bound the age of the older ice mass at 3.3-7.6 Ma from burial plus exposure ages and give a more likely 4.3-5.1 Ma from the 26Al/10Be pair for S3 and S4.
steps.quote: a more likely age for this older deposit would be 4.3–5.1 Ma

steps.action: The authors relate both ice ages to Pliocene glaciations and to the Roberts Massif record, and state that the correlation of the Middle ice is speculative.
steps.quote: possibly coincided with the early Pliocene global glaciation (ca. 4.9–4.8 Ma)

steps.action: The authors keep the claim of two stacked ice masses: Middle ice emplaced at 2.95 Ma with its rates, and an older ice mass of about 4.3-5.1 Ma in the lower core.
steps.quote: We find the age of the Middle drift ice mass to be 2.95 Ma

Mostly: boulder ages agree with the modelled age; a near-surface misfit persists under parameter variation and is attributed to mixing
Middle ice 2.95 +0.18/-0.22 Ma kept as an estimate; older ice 4.3-5.1 Ma as best explanation

end.claim: The upper section of the Ong Valley ice core was emplaced 2.95 +0.18/-0.22 Myr ago, with a sublimation rate of 22.86 m/Myr and an erosion rate of 0.206 m/Myr, and the lower section belongs to a separate, older ice mass of about 4.3-5.1 Myr.

decisive_move.sentence: The constrained fit of the forward nuclide model to the englacial units, bounded by burial ages of the recycled paleo-surface debris, yields the 2.95 Ma emplacement age and the process rates.

gates.evidence: Action: the depth-profile design (pit plus core below it, §4.1.2 ¶1) follows the forward-model approach to dating, but burial dating was 'not originally planned for' (§3 ¶5), and the authors 'had no prior reason to expect the englacial debris to be sourced from recycled surface debris' (§3 ¶4). Claim: the single-exposure model could fail and did for part of the core (§6.1 ¶2), and the boulder ages were an independent test that could have disagreed (§7.5 ¶5). However, the fitted subset and the burial constraint were chosen after the data were seen, and the S2 agreement is partly built into the fit through the burial constraint (§6.2 ¶3). Registration: the initial expectation of a single advance is described narratively (§3 ¶5), but no hypothesis, analysis or threshold is reported as fixed before the data.

Production rates by negative muon capture and fast muons (Heisinger et al. 2002a, b)
Constrained nonlinear optimization (MATLAB fmincon) with a reduced chi-square misfit

novelty_claims.quote: [...] novel dating application of cosmogenic nuclides which aims to quantify a complex exposure history of this buried ice mass.
These ancient ice masses represent new opportunities for gathering ancient climate information.
These findings provide direct evidence of an Antarctic ice sheet that was larger than present during the early and late Pliocene epoch.
[...] that exposure–burial dating of cosmogenic nuclides measured in situ in basal ice debris layers can be used for age constraint of past ice [...]

limits: No review file, open discussion, or earlier version was supplied, so only the final_paper sequence is coded. The paper went through open discussion and two anonymous referees, so the 'learning and adapting' narrative (§3 ¶5) may be a post hoc reconstruction (inference). The supplement (MATLAB code, measurement details, Fig. S2) was not available and was not inspected. Sub-claims at other statuses: the older ice mass at 4.3-5.1 Ma (bounds 3.3-7.6 Ma) is a best_explanation, and whether that ice is in situ or entrained is left unresolved. Partial vertical mixing of the supraglacial debris is a best_explanation for a systematic misfit. The correlation with Pliocene glaciations is stated by the authors as speculative. The minimum age of 1.331 Ma is an estimate under minimal assumptions. The agreement of the S2 burial age with the Middle ice age is not independent, because the burial constraint enters the fit (inference). Production-rate uncertainty is excluded from the error bounds, so the stated resolution is analytical only. The boulder check is independent data but uses the same production-rate framework (inference).
